overview: TCP gives applications an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission let it recover from loss without asking the application to assemble packets itself.
outro: The receiver buffered later data while a missing range held back delivery. Duplicate acknowledgments and a SACK block identified that hole. Retransmitting the missing 100 bytes let the receiver acknowledge the complete 300-byte stream before both sides closed.
steps: The client sends SYN and the server responds with SYN-ACK. A final ACK completes the handshake. Each side now knows the other side’s initial sequence position.
The first segment carries bytes 1 through 100. The receiver acknowledges 101, meaning it now expects that byte next.

The sender transmits two more ranges of the stream. The middle range is lost, while the later range reaches the receiver. TCP can buffer that later data without presenting an incomplete stream to the application.

The receiver keeps acknowledging 101 because that byte has not arrived. A selective acknowledgment reports the later range it already has. The sender can distinguish the missing data from buffered data.
The sender retransmits the missing range. Once it arrives, the receiver can advance its cumulative acknowledgment past all three ranges and release the contiguous stream.
A FIN says the sender has no more stream data. Both directions are acknowledged and closed independently. The endpoints then release their connection state after the appropriate closing period.
